title: Body Wisdom: A Compassionate Approach to Weight & Body Image
summary: A science-based, compassion-focused CBT program that helps you build a sustainable relationship with food, movement, and your body. Moving beyond diet culture, this program addresses the psychological roots of eating patterns, challenges body image distortions, and empowers you to make lasting changes rooted in self-care rather than self-control.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding Your Relationship with Food and Body
modules.overview: We begin by exploring your personal history with food, weight, and body image. Understanding where your patterns come from is the first step to changing them. We introduce the concept of 'Food as Medicine vs. Food as Coping.' You will learn to distinguish between physical hunger and emotional hunger. The 'Diet-Binge Cycle' is explained. We explore how restriction leads to overeating, creating a pattern that feels impossible to break. We challenge the myth that weight loss is simply about 'willpower.' You will learn about the complex biological, psychological, and social factors that influence eating behaviors. You will start a 'Food & Mood Journal.' This tracks not just what you eat, but when, why, and how you feel—revealing the emotional patterns behind eating. We introduce 'Body Image Distortion'—how your perception of your body may not match reality, and how this perception is shaped by internalized messages. Finally, we set a new goal: The aim isn't just weight loss, but building a life where food and your body are sources of joy, not anxiety.
takeaways: Eating behaviors are complex and often serve emotional needs beyond nutrition.
Restriction almost always leads to rebound eating—the body fights back.
Your relationship with food mirrors your relationship with yourself.
Body image is a mental construct, not a mirror reflection.
exercises: The Food History Timeline: Write down your earliest memory of dieting or body criticism. Track how your relationship with food and body has evolved. What patterns do you notice?
The Hunger Audit: For one day, before every eating occasion, rate your physical hunger (1-10). Also note your emotional state. Are you eating from hunger or emotion?

The Body Image Check-In: Stand in front of a mirror. List 5 things your body does for you (e.g., 'allows me to hug my children'). Then list 5 things you see that you appreciate (e.g., 'my eyes show kindness').
homework: Keep a Food & Mood Journal for 7 days. Record: time, food, hunger level (1-10), emotions before/after, and context (alone, stressed, celebrating).
Practice 'Neutral Body Language': For one week, when you catch yourself criticizing your body, say 'This is my body. It is neither good nor bad. It just is.'
Identify one 'forbidden food' and allow yourself to have it mindfully, without guilt. Notice what happens to the craving when permission is granted.

modules.title: Module 2 • Breaking the Diet-Binge Cycle: Permission and Balance
modules.overview: This module addresses the core mechanism of yo-yo dieting: The restriction-rebound cycle. We learn to break free by removing restriction. We introduce 'Regular Eating'—eating consistently throughout the day to stabilize blood sugar and prevent extreme hunger. The concept of 'Mechanical Eating' is explained. Sometimes you eat on a schedule, not just when hungry, to rebuild trust with food. We practice 'Mindful Eating'—slowing down, savoring, and paying attention to taste, texture, and satisfaction. You will learn to identify 'Satisfaction Signals.' Recognizing when food tastes good and when you've had enough. We address 'All-or-Nothing Thinking'—the belief that one 'bad' meal ruins everything. We replace this with a 'Progress, Not Perfection' mindset. Finally, we create a 'Regular Eating Schedule' tailored to your life, ensuring consistent nourishment without rigidity.
takeaways: Restriction creates obsession; permission creates peace.
Eating regularly prevents the extreme hunger that leads to overeating.
One meal does not define your health; patterns do.
Mindful eating increases satisfaction with less food.
exercises: Design Your Regular Eating Schedule: Plan 3 meals and 2-3 snacks, spaced 3-4 hours apart. Write down approximate times that fit your life.
The Mindful Meal: Choose one meal this week. Eat it without distractions. Put your fork down between bites. Chew 20 times. Notice flavors, textures, satisfaction. How does it feel different?
The Permission Experiment: Make a list of 5 'forbidden' foods. This week, allow yourself to have each one, mindfully, without guilt. Notice if the obsession decreases.
homework: Follow your Regular Eating Schedule for 7 days, even if you're not hungry. Notice how this affects your evening cravings.
Practice Mindful Eating for at least one meal per day. Start with 5 minutes of focused attention, then allow yourself to eat normally.
When you catch yourself in 'All-or-Nothing' thinking ('I ate a cookie, the day is ruined'), stop and say 'One cookie is just one cookie. I can continue making choices that serve me.'

modules.title: Module 3 • Emotional Eating: Finding Alternatives to Food
modules.overview: This module explores the emotional function of eating. Food often serves as a coping mechanism for stress, sadness, boredom, or anxiety. We identify your personal 'Emotional Eating Triggers'—specific situations, emotions, or thoughts that lead to eating when not physically hungry. You will learn to create an 'Emotional Eating Toolkit'—alternative coping strategies for each trigger. We practice 'Urge Surfing'—riding out the wave of an emotional eating urge without acting on it. The concept of 'Emotional Awareness' is introduced. Learning to name and sit with difficult emotions instead of numbing them with food. We explore 'Self-Soothing' techniques that provide comfort without calories—breathing, movement, connection, creativity. Finally, we address 'Comfort Eating'—recognizing that sometimes eating for comfort is okay, but having other tools expands your options.
takeaways: Emotional eating serves a purpose; understanding that purpose helps you find alternatives.
You cannot eliminate emotional eating entirely, but you can reduce its frequency and impact.
Sitting with difficult emotions is uncomfortable but necessary for growth.
Having multiple coping tools prevents over-reliance on food.
exercises: The Trigger Inventory: List 10 situations, emotions, or thoughts that trigger emotional eating. Be specific (e.g., 'Sunday afternoon boredom,' 'after an argument with my partner').
Build Your Toolkit: For each trigger, brainstorm 3 non-food alternatives. Mix strategies: movement (walk), connection (call a friend), creativity (draw), self-care (bath), distraction (puzzle).

Urge Surfing Practice: Next time you feel an emotional eating urge, set a timer for 10 minutes. During that time, do not eat. Notice the urge. Breathe. Write down what you're feeling. After 10 minutes, decide if you still want to eat.
homework: For one week, when you feel an emotional eating urge, pause. Name the emotion ('I'm feeling stressed'). Choose a tool from your toolkit. Try it for 10 minutes before deciding whether to eat.
Practice Urge Surfing 3 times this week. After each time, journal: What emotion was I feeling? Did the urge pass? What did I learn?
Create a 'Comfort Menu'—a list of 10 non-food comforts you can turn to when you need soothing (e.g., 'wrap in a blanket and read,' 'take a hot shower,' 'call my sister').

modules.title: Module 4 • Body Image Restructuring: Seeing Yourself Clearly
modules.overview: This module addresses the mental and emotional aspects of body image. How you think about your body affects how you feel about it. We explore 'Body Checking' behaviors—constantly weighing, measuring, or examining your body. These behaviors reinforce body dissatisfaction. You will learn to identify 'Body Image Distortions'—thoughts about your body that are exaggerated or untrue. We practice 'Cognitive Restructuring' for body image—challenging negative thoughts with balanced, compassionate alternatives. The concept of 'Body Neutrality' is introduced. Moving from body hatred, through body acceptance, toward body neutrality (your body is neither good nor bad, it just is). We explore 'Body Functionality'—appreciating what your body can do rather than focusing solely on appearance. Finally, we address 'Social Comparison'—how comparing yourself to others (or to past versions of yourself) fuels body dissatisfaction.
takeaways: Body image is a mental construct, heavily influenced by thoughts and behaviors.
Body checking reinforces dissatisfaction; reducing it improves body image.
You can change how you think about your body without changing your body.
Body neutrality is often more achievable than body love.
exercises: The Body Checking Audit: List all the ways you check your body (weighing, measuring, mirror checking, clothes trying-on). For one week, reduce these by 50%. Notice how this affects your mood.
Body Image Thought Record: When you have a negative body thought ('My stomach is huge'), write it down. Challenge it: 'Is this thought helpful? Is it true? What's a more balanced thought?'
Functionality Appreciation: Each day this week, write down one thing your body allowed you to do (e.g., 'carried groceries,' 'hugged my child,' 'felt the sun on my skin').
homework: Reduce body checking behaviors by 50% for 7 days. When you catch yourself checking, pause and say 'This is not helpful. I'm going to focus on something else.'
Practice Body Neutrality Statements: When you have a negative body thought, replace it with a neutral one ('My body is my body. It serves me. That's enough.').
Create a 'Body Functionality List'—20 things your body allows you to do. Read this list when body image is difficult.

modules.title: Module 5 • Sustainable Movement: Joyful Activity, Not Punishment
modules.overview: This module reframes exercise from punishment for eating to celebration of what your body can do. We explore 'Movement for Joy'—finding activities you actually enjoy, not ones you think you 'should' do. The concept of 'Intuitive Movement' is introduced. Moving your body in ways that feel good, not based on calories burned. We address 'Exercise as Compensation'—the belief that you must 'earn' food through exercise. We replace this with movement as self-care. You will learn to identify your 'Movement Preferences'—what types of activity feel good in your body. We practice 'Gentle Movement'—incorporating activity without the all-or-nothing mindset that leads to injury or burnout. Finally, we create a 'Sustainable Movement Plan' that fits your life, preferences, and current fitness level.
takeaways: Movement should feel good, not like punishment.
You don't need to exercise to 'earn' food—food is not a reward.
Sustainable movement is consistent, not intense.
Finding joy in movement makes it easier to maintain.
exercises: The Movement Experiment: Try 3 different types of movement this week (e.g., dance class, nature walk, yoga video). Rate each: enjoyment (1-10), how your body felt, likelihood to continue.
The Compensation Challenge: For one week, do not use exercise to 'earn' food. Eat based on hunger and satisfaction. Move based on what feels good. Notice the difference.
Design Your Movement Plan: Create a flexible weekly plan with 3-5 movement sessions. Mix types (strength, cardio, flexibility, rest). Make it realistic and enjoyable.
homework: Engage in movement 3-4 times this week, choosing activities you enjoy. Notice how movement affects your mood and energy, not just your weight.
Practice Intuitive Movement: Before each session, check in with your body. What does it want? Gentle stretching? A brisk walk? Rest? Honor that.
Reframe Exercise Thoughts: When you think 'I should exercise,' replace it with 'I get to move my body today.' Notice how this changes your motivation.

modules.title: Module 6 • Long-Term Maintenance: Building a Life You Love
modules.overview: The final module focuses on maintaining progress and handling setbacks. We acknowledge that change is not linear. We explore 'Lapse vs. Relapse'—understanding that one difficult day or week doesn't mean you've failed. You will create a 'Maintenance Toolkit'—strategies to return to when you feel yourself slipping into old patterns. We practice 'Self-Compassion'—treating yourself with kindness when you struggle, not criticism. The concept of 'Progress, Not Perfection' is reinforced. Celebrating small wins and learning from challenges. We address 'Social Support'—building a network of people who support your journey without enabling diet culture. Finally, we write a 'Body Wisdom Manifesto'—a personal statement of your values and intentions for your relationship with food and body going forward.
takeaways: Setbacks are normal and expected; they don't mean failure.
Self-compassion is more effective than self-criticism for long-term change.
Progress is measured in behaviors and mindset, not just weight.
You have the tools to handle any challenge that arises.
exercises: The Maintenance Toolkit: List 5 strategies from this program that work best for you. Write them on a card. Keep it visible. When you struggle, return to these tools.
The Lapse Plan: Write down: 'If I have a difficult day/week, I will...' (e.g., 'pause and breathe,' 'review my manifesto,' 'reach out to support,' 'return to regular eating').
Write Your Body Wisdom Manifesto: In 200-300 words, write your personal statement about your relationship with food, body, and self. Include your values, intentions, and commitments.
homework: Review your Maintenance Toolkit weekly. Add new tools as you discover them. Remove tools that don't work for you.
Practice Self-Compassion Daily: When you struggle, say 'This is hard. I'm doing my best. I can learn from this and continue.'
Share your Body Wisdom Manifesto with someone you trust. Ask them to remind you of it when you forget.
Continue your Food & Mood Journal, but reduce frequency to 2-3 times per week. Use it as a check-in tool, not a daily requirement.

Celebrate your progress. Make a list of 10 ways you've changed (e.g., 'I eat breakfast regularly,' 'I'm kinder to my body,' 'I have tools for emotional eating'). Read this when you doubt your progress.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
